page: Microsoft Azure E8s_v4 is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance powered by an Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL processor operating at a base frequency of 2.6 GHz. Based on the x86_64 architecture, the instance provides 8 virtual CPUs mapped across 4 dedicated physical cores with hyperthreading enabled. It incorporates 35 MB of L3 cache alongside support for instruction sets including AVX-512 with VNNI, AES cryptography, and BMI2. The instance lacks bundled local ephemeral storage and includes zero GPUs, relying entirely on attached remote network volumes for disk persistence.

The defining architectural attribute of the E8s_v4 is its memory allocation, featuring 64.0 GB of system memory, which establishes an 8:1 RAM-to-vCPU ratio. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate consistent mid-tier performance across synthetic compute and system metrics, with Geekbench multi-core scoring 4,503 and PassMark CPU scoring 8,469.96. While cached small-block memory throughput reaches an average 403.65 GB/sec, uncached large-block throughput drops into the lower quartile at 29.42 GB/sec read and 24.3 GB/sec write. Computational tasks executing single-core operations also register in the lower quartile, whereas parallelized workflows exhibit average throughput.

From an infrastructure investment standpoint, the E8s_v4 trades aggressive compute throughput and local high-speed storage for memory capacity per core. Application-level testing reflects solid transactional utility for memory-resident workloads, achieving 6.72 million Redis SET operations per second and 6.43 GB/sec in static web serving throughput. Conversely, resource-intensive generation tasks such as 7B-parameter LLM inference register poor output rates, confirming that the instance is ill-suited for heavy arithmetic processing.

The Microsoft Azure E8s_v4 is best aligned with memory-constrained enterprise deployments that do not require high sustained CPU clocks. Ideal workloads include medium-sized in-memory databases, Redis caching layers, enterprise backend services, data indexing engines, and relational database management systems that benefit directly from high memory-to-vCPU density.
